Technical report: AI-Based Interactive Quantum-Algorithm Learning Platform

Team Chica (PE-B65-13), batch 76, faculty Sonal Kukreja. Problem S18 [SIH26140], Egreen Quanta. Repository: https://github.com/KingKartik9666/Prompt_Project

1. Architecture. A learner question and a level (beginner or intermediate) go through four prompts in code/workflow.py:

  1. P1 Router returns JSON with the algorithm, parameters, intent, false premise, language and an injection flag. Out-of-scope messages get a redirect; injection attempts are flagged and logged.
  2. P2 Explainer returns JSON steps with the state after each step.
  3. P3 Claim extractor copies the final probabilities, and quantum_sim.py (a NumPy statevector) compares them with the simulation, with a tolerance of 0.02. On a mismatch, P2 is called once more with the simulator's feedback.
  4. P4 Practice writes one question with a hint, an answer key and a self-review.

Verifiable algorithms: Bell state, Deutsch-Jozsa, and Grover on 2 qubits. Others are explained and labelled unverified.

2. Tools and models.

  • Python, NumPy and the google-genai SDK.
  • The prototype runs Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite (gemini-3.5-flash-lite). Our runs were local; the notebook also opens in Colab (key in Colab Secrets) and runs in Docker.
  • Because of free-tier quotas, all tests were also run on Claude Opus 5.5, with one fresh Claude Code subagent per LLM call (step_runner.py) and the same code-side checks.

3. Prompt design.

PromptTemp.Techniques
P1 Router0.0Fixed labels, JSON schema, learner text inside <message> tags (treated as data), injection flag
P2 Explainer0.2Chain-of-thought (state after every step), audience-aware rules per level, 2 few-shot examples, JSON, verifier-feedback slot
P3 Claim extractor0.0Narrow role: copy claims, never fix numbers; JSON. The check itself is done by code
P4 Practice0.4Draft, then answer key and hint, then self-review; JSON

The explainer was iterated v1 (one line) → v2 (role, level, fixed sections) → v3 (few-shot, JSON, temperature 0.2) → final (+ intent, DJ rule, repair slot). Results on Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, 12 runs each:

  • Final probabilities verified: 5/12 → 12/12 → 12/12 (one v2 Deutsch-Jozsa answer was physically wrong but passed the P(00)-only check).
  • Clean JSON: 0 → 0 → 12/12.
  • Average length: 615 → 394 → 178 words.

4. Test results (13 inputs: 6 Normal, 5 Edge, 2 Invalid). The rubric is applied by a Claude grader agent (LLM-assisted).

ModelAutomatic checksRubric: Pass / Partial / FailVerified on first attempt
Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite (prototype)12/134 / 5 / 48/8
Claude Opus 5.5 (cross-check)13/137 / 6 / 09/9

Gemini failures:

  • A compare question was misrouted, so it was not verified.
  • One practice key is wrong, even though P4's self-review said it was correct.
  • One intermediate state is unnormalised.
  • One unverifiable Shor answer has a wrong state.

The false premise, Hinglish, injection and invalid inputs were all handled correctly. The repair retry never fired: on every verifiable answer, the final probabilities matched the simulator on the first attempt (intermediate states are not checked; test 3 had an unnormalised one). A scripted test (test_repair.py) confirms its code path.

5. Limitations.

  • Only the explanation's final probabilities are checked: not the intermediate states, not P4's key, and only P(00) for Deutsch-Jozsa.
  • Only three small algorithms can be verified.
  • The rubric grader is an LLM, and there is no learner feedback yet.
  • Free-tier quotas limited the number of repeats.

Next: check each step state and the practice key with the simulator, extend the simulator, grade a sample by hand, and run a small trial with classmates.

6. Responsible use. No personal data is collected. Questions go to Google's Gemini API, so learners should not type personal details. The key is never in the code or the repository. The tool is a learning aid, not a replacement for a teacher. Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) wrote most of the code, the prompt drafts, the test cases, the rubric and the report drafts; the team chose the problem and scope, made the design decisions and is responsible for the submission. All results come from our saved runs.
